answer: Use the clock command. Set the zone with 'set clock timezone <value>', for example 'set clock timezone Beijing-Chongqing-Hong_Kong-Urumqi[GMT+08:00]'; the value comes from the fixed list of named zones (International Date Line West[GMT-12:00] through Kiritimati[GMT+14:00]), and the default is Universal-Time-Coordinated. To see where time comes from, use 'show clock time-source': ntp means the NE synchronises via NTP, manual means it uses its own internal clock. Default is manual. The same show also returns current-time, universal-time, timezone, uptime, uptime-seconds, DST-active (default false) and last-time-jump (format '<time1> to <time2>'; jumps under 10 seconds are ignored). If DNS is not properly configured, show clock can take up to 2 minutes to respond. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. Use 'set ne node-type OADM'. node-type takes ILA, OADM or XPDR, and it can only be set or changed on a 1830 GX G34c chassis, which defaults to ILA; G31/G32 default to OADM and G42 to XPDR. G34c support for OADM starts at R7.0 (in R6.x it was ILA only). Preconditions for setting OADM: no OMS monitoring-mode in the system may be 'ila-with-equalization' or 'not-monitored', that is no spectrum (or ochm) objects may exist, and no direction-* may exist. Going the other way, to set ILA: no OMS monitoring-mode on the dwdm-line ports may be 'intrusive' (no RD or PAx card present), and no degree, no oxcon and no nmc may exist. Note also that G34c SLTE mode (l0-mode-op slte) is supported only when node-type is ILA.

'show ne-function'. It takes no parameters and runs in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. It lists the NE generic functions in one output, that is the directions and the amplifiers of the node. A G30 example returns direction-1 through direction-8, then amplifier-raman-1-7, amplifier-1-1-A, amplifier-1-1-B, amplifier-1-3.1-drop, amplifier-1-5-A, amplifier-1-5-B, amplifier-2-1-A, amplifier-2-1-B, amplifier-2-3-A, amplifier-2-3-B, and finally ne-function itself.

Use the ntp command: 'set ntp ntp-enabled true ntp-auth-enabled true'. ntp-enabled is true by default; ntp-auth-enabled is false by default, so authentication must be turned on explicitly. The third settable attribute is assignment-method, which selects which configured values the system uses: manual, dhcp or both, defaulting to both. 'show ntp' returns ntp-enabled, ntp-auth-enabled, ntp-active-server (the currently active NTP server) and assignment-method. The ntp object is system managed and cannot be manually added or deleted. To complete authentication you also need a key (add ntp-key-<key-id> with is-trusted true) and the server association (set ntp-server-<ip-address> auth-key-id <id>). Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

NTP keys are managed with 'add ntp-key-<key-id> key-type <value> key-value <value> [is-trusted <value>]', plus set, show and delete on the same AID. key-type, the hash algorithm used for NTP message digest computation, accepts sha-1, aes-cmac, sha-256 or md5, with no default. key-id is a number in the range 1..65534. key-value is a string of length 8..40. is-trusted marks the key as a trusted NTP key and takes true or false, defaulting to false. Example: 'add ntp-key-2 is-trusted true key-type sha-1 key-value Infinera'. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. The origin attribute records the NTP address assignment method and a DHCP-configured NTP entry can be converted into a manually configured one simply by changing it: 'set ntp-server-<ip-address> origin manual'. origin takes dhcp (address assigned to the system by a DHCP server) or manual (address manually configured); the default is manual. The ip-address key may be an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address or a DNS domain name. The other settable attributes on the entry are auth-key-id (a uint32 key id, or not-applicable, which is the default), label (0..256 characters), admin-state (lock, unlock or maintenance, default unlock) and alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed). show also returns oper-state (default disabled) and avail-state.

Use 'show ntp-server-status-<ip-address>', for example 'show ntp-server-status-172.19.13.218'. The key field is reach: an 8-bit shift register holding the outcome of recent probes, with the most recent probe in the 2^0 position; the value 377 means all the recent probes have been answered. Supporting fields are when (seconds since the last packet was received), poll (polling interval in seconds), delay (path delay in ms), offset (clock offset to the peer in ms), jitter (path jitter in ms), stratum of the remote peer, refid (reference clock type or address), type (local, unicast, multicast or broadcast), auth-status (ok, yes, bad or none, default none) and condition (for example sys.peer, reject, candidate).

Syntax is 'restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>]'. If <type> is omitted a warm start is done by default. warm reboots the processor of the CHM6, UCM4, etc. and is non service affecting; the system regains connectivity within five minutes, and a warm reboot of an XMM4 is non-service affecting but visibility is lost for 3 minutes. cold reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting, also regaining connectivity within five minutes; a cold reboot of XMM4 is not service affecting but visibility is lost. A third type, shutdown, gracefully shuts the card down. Restartable entities: card (cold, warm, shutdown), card sub-component (cold, warm) and tom (cold); not all cards support all restart types. Omitting <resource-id> restarts the active controller card. The command asks for confirmation unless -f is given.

Because set-time is only applicable when time-source is manual, that is when NTP is not enabled. Check with 'show clock time-source' (values ntp or manual, default manual); if it reads ntp, disable synchronisation with 'set ntp ntp-enabled false' before setting the clock by hand. The new time uses a format derived from ISO 8601 with combined date and time, where Z is the UTC timezone, for example 'set-time 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z'; a non-UTC timezone is allowed by supplying +/-hh:mm instead of Z, for example 'set-time 2021-04-01T18:46:44+03:00'. Retrieve the current system time with the 'time' command, which reports it in the system configured timezone rather than the timezone used in the set-time command. set-time runs in Operational Mode.

Yes, 'status equipment'. The Equipment dashboard summarises all equipment in the system with relevant details like temperature and power usage: the list of chassis, the cards per chassis and their subtype, the toms per card, and per-equipment data including temperature sensors, power values and generic status (presence or absence, oper state, alarms). The default scope is the entire network element. On a large NE you can filter to a single chassis by passing the chassis id, for example 'status equipment 5'; only existing chassis ids are accepted and wildcards are not supported, so it is either all chassis or exactly one. Output uses symbols: a check for oper-state enabled, admin-state unlocked or no alarms, a cross for oper-state disabled, and a padlock for admin-state lock. Access: Operational mode.

Use 'clear [-f] system [[action=]<value>] [[restart-behavior=]<value>] [type=]<value> [[target=]<value>]'. The clear system command wipes the system or a specific instance back to factory configuration and performs a secure wipe of the system data. type takes factory-reset (resets the system or a particular equipment to factory configuration, stopping target traffic services and removing files and user configurations, which may imply loss of connectivity), full-wipe (cleans the entire system and reinstalls SW on controller and line-cards; a base software reinstall from ONIE is required to recover) or inactive (clears the inactive software partition). target may be the entire system or a chassis/card AID; if omitted the entire system is cleared. restart-behavior is a standard restart (default) or shutdown. Limits: factory-reset does not take effect for G30 Optical Carrier-Cards (OCC2T, OCC2E) but is supported for the G30 controller card (FRCU), and clear system factory-reset with the shutdown option is not supported on L0 cards. Example: 'clear system factory-reset shutdown'. For a simple database wipe use 'clear database' instead.

Type 'time'. It takes no parameters, runs in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode, and prints the system's time in a single line, for example '2020-06-29T22:29:37+00:00'. It reports the time based on the system configured timezone. For more detail use 'show clock current-time', which also gives universal-time, timezone, uptime, time-source, DST-active and last-time-jump, though show clock can take up to 2 minutes to respond if DNS is not properly configured.

The 'uptime' command displays the system uptime and load average, for example '21:24:09 up 41 days, 15:56, 1 user, load average: 0.10, 0.35, 0.39'. The load average, also called average system load, indicates whether there are multiple tasks queued on the system (on the card). Whether it is high or low depends on the number of cores the system has, how many CPUs are integrated into the system (card), and the load average number itself. The rule to judge it: a load average value is considered high when it is greater than the number of CPUs on the card. The command takes no parameters and runs in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. 'manual-switchover [-f] [resource=]<value>' takes the AID of the object to be switched, and the command warns before proceeding: 'Controller will switchover and connection to the management interface will be lost. Do you want to continue? [y/n]'. You confirm at that prompt to proceed with the manual switch operation, or pass -f to force the command without confirmation. Example AIDs by chassis: 'manual-switchover card-1-3' on a G42, 'manual-switchover card-1-5' on a G32, and 'manual-switchover card-1-12' on a G34c. Access: Operational mode. For the full procedure the guide refers to the 1830 GX Software Management Procedures Guide.

'show protection'. It takes no parameters and displays the node's protection container, that is the protection setting. Access: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The related objects underneath it have their own commands: 'show protection-group-<name>' for a group and its state and timers, and 'show protection-unit-<protection-group-name>/<protection-unit-name>' for an individual member.

On protection-group, switching-mode defaults to unidirectional and accepts unidirectional or bidirectional. The wait-to-restore timer is wtr-timer: it is the trigger clearance soaking time before reverting to the working protection unit, measured and set in 1-second steps, range 60..720 seconds, default 300. It only applies in revertive mode, and reversion-mode itself defaults to non-revertive (values revertive, non-revertive), so you must set reversion-mode revertive for the WTR timer to take effect. The related read-only remaining-wtr shows the remaining WTR time in the range 0..720 seconds. The separate hold-off-timer is the switching trigger soaking time before switching, in 1-millisecond steps, range 0..10000 ms, default 0.

Use the operating command 'protection-switch [-f] [operation-type=]<value> [switch-target=]<value> [protection-group=]<value>'. For a force to the protection path: 'protection-switch protection-group-test operation-type=force switch-target=protection'. operation-type takes force, lockout, manual or release; switch-target is the target of the switch command and is not needed for the release and lockout operations. -f forces the command without confirmation. Access: Operational mode. The equivalent configured request is the protection-group pg-request attribute, which accepts clear (the default), manual-to-working, manual-to-protection, forced-to-working, forced-to-protection, protection-lockout and exercise (exercise applies only to bidirectional SNCP).

Use 'show protection-unit-<protection-group-name>/<protection-unit-name> [AID] [transport-entity] [state] [role] [alarm-report-control] [label]'. The state attribute is the one that tells you which member is carrying traffic: it takes active, standby, available or unknown. role tells you which member is which in the pair, taking working or protection. transport-entity gives the instance identifier of the underlying transport entity, and AID the object identifier. At group level, 'show protection-group-<name> pg-state' and last-switch-trigger show the switching state and what caused the last switchover. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Most alarms have both an automatic raise criteria and a clear criteria, but a very small subset have no clear criteria and instead require the user to acknowledge and clear them manually. Use 'clear [-f] alarm [alarm-type=]<value> [[resource=]<value>[,<value>]*]', for example 'clear alarm DBRESTOREFAIL'; -f forces the command without confirmation. To find which alarms qualify, list the inventory entries that have can-be-cleared-by-user = true: 'show alarm-inventory can-be-cleared-by-user=true'. This mechanism applies only to system alarms that are not associated with any particular resource but with the system itself, that is system wide or global alarms. Access: Operational mode. To acknowledge rather than clear, use 'set-alarm-state ack ...'.

That is governed by arc-behavior on the alarm-control object, the system wide alarm-reporting-control behavior switch. It takes leave-alarms, which when ARC is set to inhibit leaves the current alarms in a raised mode, or clear-alarms, which when ARC is set to inhibit clears the current alarms. The default is leave-alarms, so by default the already-raised alarms stay up. Change it with 'set alarm-control arc-behavior clear-alarms' or 'set alarm-control arc-behavior leave-alarms', and check with 'show alarm-control'. The same object carries alarm-soaking-behavior, taking automatic (soaking time defined in the FM profile) or no-soak (certain alarms specified in the FM profile have no soaking time), default automatic. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Look it up in the alarm inventory, which holds all possible alarm types for the system with static information for each: 'show alarm-inventory-<alarm-type> [resource-type] [alarm-category] [alarm-type-description] [corrective-action] [default-severity] [service-affecting]', for example 'show alarm-inventory-TIM' or 'show alarm-inventory-MSIM'. alarm-type-description gives the description of the alarm type (string 0..128) and corrective-action gives system provided information on how to correct the situation that triggered it (string 0..256). alarm-category takes communication, facility, equipment, environmental, processing-error, software, quality-of-service or security. default-severity lists the possible default severities (critical, major, minor, warning, not-reported, event), which can differ by resource-type, and service-affecting takes indeterminate, sa, nsa or sa-nsa.

Yes, that is exactly what alarm-severity-entry is for: it configures the severity for one particular alarm. Use 'set alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location> severity <value>'. resource-type is the type to be modified (for example CHM1R, FAN, 1830 GX G31), alarm-type is the abbreviated alarm code (for example ADMIN-LOCK, BERSD), direction is na, ingress or egress, and location is na, near-end or far-end. severity takes critical, event, major, minor, not-reported or warning. Examples: 'set alarm-severity-entry-OTU2/TIM/ingress/near-end severity minor' and 'set alarm-severity-entry-tom/EQPTCOMFAIL severity major'. Read it back with the matching show, which also returns service-affecting. Press ? after the command to list the available entities. The object is system managed and cannot be manually deleted.

alarm-severity-entry addresses one specific alarm through the four-part key <resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location>, for example 'set alarm-severity-entry-OTU2/TIM/ingress/near-end severity minor'. alarm-severity-profile instead sets the severity for an alarm profile entry: 'set alarm-severity-profile <profile-entry> severity <critical|event|major|minor|not-reported|warning>', for example 'set alarm-severity-profile alarm-severity-entry-trusted-certificate/CERTIFICATE-EXPIRED severity critical'. Both take the same severity value set, and both objects are managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Use 'show alarm-severity-profile' to view the profiles, and press ? after 'set alarm-severity-profile' to display the list of available profiles. Access for both: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use 'show current-alarms [number-of-alarms] [last-changed]'. number-of-alarms is the count of currently raised alarms, and last-changed is the timestamp of the last change in the current alarm list, covering either a raise or a clear event. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. For a breakdown by severity instead of a bare count, the System dashboard from the 'status' command includes an alarm summary giving the number of alarms per severity, for example '13 current alarms (1 critical, 5 major, 2 not-reported, 5 minor)'. The full list itself comes from 'show alarms'.

Look in the conditions with the 'get-conditions' command. A condition is an alarm that is not considered current, which happens when the alarm severity is configured as not-reported or not-alarmed, when the alarm is suppressed due to alarm correlation, when it is suppressed due to ARC (alarm reporting control), or when it is suppressed due to AINS. Syntax: 'get-conditions [[direction=]<value>] [[resource=]<value>] [[resource-type=]<value>] [[alarm-type=]<value>] [[location=]<value>] [[AID=]<value>]'. direction takes all, na, ingress or egress and defaults to all; location takes all, na, near-end or far-end and defaults to all; resource, resource-type, alarm-type and AID narrow the search further. Access: Operational mode.
